If you're on a budget, consider building your own alarm system as opposed to spending on an ADT or another monthly-fine service. If you're not technically inclined, poke around Ebay for some cheap DIY pre-configured systems. If you are technical, an Arduino with 433mhz sensors, some NinjaBlocks code, and a 20-pack of Ebay magnetic door sensors (they work on windows too) will set you back about $125 total. A Pi can do the same thing with a bit of Python, and has the added benefit of being able to text/email you alerts.

Another super simple and immediately-available option is a door-stop alarm (http://www.amazon.com/GE-Personal-Security-Door-Alarm/dp/B0000YNR4M).

There are plenty of non-alarm options as well. First, understand the nature of home burglaries and those who commit them, and to plan around their skills. Start with this, it's super recent: http://www.bbc.com/future/story/20150618-the-strange-expertise-of-burglars

Some specific suggestions might also include:

Turn your locks/deadbolts upside down so that the "teeth" of your keys face downward. This makes your locks 10x more difficult to pick (while most crooks kick, the ones that get away with it pick). Make sure all of your doors are solid-core (a lot of landlords skip on this) and have a solid lock. Window bars aren't unreasonably expensive, and after an incident like yours are something that many landlords are amenable to installing at their cost.

Put some "protected by ADT" signs/stickers on door entrances and back/side windows. Put big dog toys on your back porch, and maybe a pet carrier where it can be seen in a garage/storage area, even if you don't have a dog (but also get a dog, their whole life is to stop people from messing with you).

Put a couple of lamps on electronic timers in visible windows with random on/off times to prevent being cased. Putting something like this in a guest bedroom can easily give the impression of a night owl working in an office even when you're not home.

One of my favorites - install cheap solar-powered motion-sensor lights in non-standard places (such as at the back of a fence or at ankle-level near your doors). This plays heavily into the suggestions of the BBC article - get the crook out of their element and disrupt their flow. Also, outside light is the single best deterrent to common crime anywhere, ever. (http://www.amazon.com/LuckLED-Outdoor-Detection-Sensing-Function/dp/B00VUHJQEI).

Leave your porch lights on all the time. Install brighter lights. The vast majority of home criminals only work in the dark.

Keep a TV on a timer when away. Anyone getting too close to the house in the evenings should hear The Golden Girls at an inappropriately-loud level.

Don't mention on social media when you're away from home. Don't let your family post that kind of thing either. Most people don't realize that all of us know a burglar or a burglar-to-be, and amateurs often start by taking things they've seen before.

Good luck. Real security often takes a lot of work and preparation, but just finding one or two weak points and putting obstacles on them can do wonders for your peace of mind!

The storm over the removal of the Nobel laureate has yielded some vital evidence

After more than a month of bitter debate, Sir Paul Nurse, the president of the Royal Society, tried to bring an end to the controversy over Sir Tim Hunt with almost as few words as it started.

“It became a complete Twitter and media storm,” he said firmly on Radio 4’s Broadcasting House. “He should never have been sacked by University College London.”

This was an extraordinary vindication for Sir Tim, and must have caused acute embarrassment to UCL. For weeks, all eyes had been focused on them. Would they do the right thing? It was after the Today show broadcast on June 10 that the establishment there had decided to make an example of the Nobel laureate who’d donated his time to their students. Connie St Louis, the journalist who gave her version of Sir Tim’s toast, to a lunch for women in science last month, described the horror with which his demeaning of women in science was received. “There was a deathly silence,” she said. “Nobody was laughing . . . these guys are incredibly upset. And so after he’d finished, there was just this deathly, deathly silence.”

That did sound bad. And Ms St Louis drove home her point on BBC television. “It was a room of about a hundred people.” she said. “Nobody was laughing . . . everybody was stony-faced.”

It now seems clear that the toast was a joke, if not a very good one. The Times first broke the story of a report, by a European Commission official who had been there, describing the second part of Sir Tim’s speech; he had said “Now, seriously . . .” and gone on to praise women scientists in Korea, ending by saying that they should “do science, despite all the obstacles, and despite monsters like me”.

The EU report said it gave a transcript “as precise as I can recall”. Public opinion shifted decisively after the report came out. Old man makes bad joke, so what? Nobel laureates defended Sir Tim to this paper. This was embarrassing to Hunt’s critics, especially perhaps to David Colquhoun of UCL and the Royal Society’s diversity committee, who had called Sir Tim “the misogynistic Nobel prize winner” on Twitter.

It is not clear why it is so wrong to be either old or male, but in any case women scientists — and ethnic minority scientists — protested in droves that Sir Tim was no sexist. Hyunsook Lee of Korea wrote that Sir Tim had mentored her for the last 15 years and would continue to do so. Trish Greenhalgh of Oxford said that when she had been “a mouthy 17-year-old” Sir Tim to her she would “make a great scientist. He gave me a place at Cambridge.”

Maria Leptin, the director of the European Molecular Biology Organisation, wrote: “Tim Hunt chaired the selection panel appointing the first female head of the EMBO. Full disclosure: me.”

Sir Tim had even successfully pushed for a crèche at the Okinawa Institute. Sexist? Few in the rarefied world of senior scientists, it turned out, had ever done as much for women.

The British public were behind Sir Tim. On one negative newspaper article about him, the accompanying online poll received 25,000 responses; 86 per cent supported Sir Tim.

Still Ms St Louis insisted on her version of events: a serious advocation of segregation in the lab, stony faces, deathly silence. And UCL were not to be swayed. They had condemned Sir Tim on the basis of a tweet, a hashtag from the online feminist magazine Vagenda and Ms St Louis’s description of the shock in the room as Sir Tim offended everybody present.

Professor Nurse’s blistering comments on the Twitter storm, and his condemnation of UCL, were an extraordinary vindication of this ally of women in science. As Britain’s most senior scientist, his view counted far more than that of a universitythat was being mocked around the world.

He will be glad he had the good sense to believe his friend. Today The Times published an audio recording of the end of Sir Tim’s speech. It will be embarrassing for those who persecuted him without even the most basic fact-checking. Sir Tim’s self-deprecating tone is unmistakable: as he has always maintained, he was poking fun at himself.

“Congratulations, everybody,” he says warmly. “I do hope there is nothing holding you back, especially monsters like me.’

There is laughter in the room and the first clap is heard before the snippet ends. What the reaction will be in the common rooms of UCL is difficult to predict — but I suspect that “deathly silence” is not going to cover it.

Louise Mensch is a journalist and former Conservative MP. Natalia Demina is a Russian science journalist
